articleTitle: Standardization of transformers
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Generally speaking standardization in any sphere is a means whereby maintenance can be simplified, costs reduced, productivity increased, production stabilized, and availability assured. One sphere where it could be beneficially applied is the one that we are discussing tonight — distribution transformers. As pointed out earlier, the Republic's annual requirements of transformers is about 2 000. While this number is large enough to justify local manufacture it is dangerously near the lower limit for economic production because of the number of factories operating in the Republic. This means that everything must be done to help the manufacturer obtain reasonably economical production runs. Standardizing of tanks, cores, conservators, windings, and insulator bushings by reducing the variety produced must of necessity keep costs down. In a competitive field such as exists in transformer manufacture, these lower manufacturing costs are passed on to the consumer together with the further advantages of simplified purchasing, short delivery times and ease of replacement.

articleTitle: Modern high-voltage circuit breakers
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The paper reviews the ever increasing severity of the duty imposed on the modern high-voltage circuit breaker by the never ending increase in size and capacity of transmission networks. 500 kV lines are already in service in Russia, and there and elsewhere the possibilities of even higher voltages are being earnestly studied. Load currents of 4000 amp and fault currents of 60 kA are an immediate requirement and at such fault currents the ‘line-side’ or kilometric fault overshadows the busbar fault.

articleTitle: Symposium on distribution transformers
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The majority of electrical engineers are concerned with the distribution of electricity in some form or other. Probably the most important component on such systems is the distribution transformer. It has been estimated that there are about 24 000 of these in the Republic and the annual increase is at present about 2000. This has resulted in the development of a healthy local manufacturing industry. It has also made the general subject of transformers all the more interesting since the members of our Institute now include those directly concerned with all aspects from manufacture to maintenance. At the same time, because there are so many firms manufacturing transformers and so many supply authorities ordering, installing, and maintaining them, there is a relatively wide divergence of opinion on many features concerning this apparently simple bit of apparatus.

abstract: This book is an outcome of the six Christmas lectures at the Royal Institution delivered to school children by the author; Dr Allibone is a well-known authority on the subject, and the book is an excellent survey of the field from earliest to very recent times. It is intended for the interested layman, but the more serious student who seeks an overall picture before going into detail will learn much from it. The book is very well illustrated, and this adds considerably to its enjoyment. Beginning with fuel from coal, Dr Allibone traces the history of important nuclear discoveries from Dalton and Faraday. A chapter is devoted to the atom and another to the nucleus. Several interesting experiments at the lectures are described and they enrich ones understanding of the subject. Next fission of uranium, nuclear power stations, the production and uses of isotopes, and power from fusion are dealt with. The book constitutes an admirable summary of basic essentials to date. — R.K.

articleTitle: Discussion
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: In the United States and Scandinavia distribution transformers are routine impulse tested which, in addition to proving that the transformers are capable of withstanding the surge levels, serves also as a check of workmanship. We are far from reaching this stage in this country but more regular impulse testing, e.g. batch testing, as mentioned in one paper, may have to be considered for large orders of distribution transformers in this country when adequate impulse testing facilities are available. One author suggests that impulse testing might replace what he calls ‘the onerous induced-voltage test’ which seems to presuppose that this test is more severe than the impulse test. This viewpoint is not entirely shared and I think that it is true to say that for disc-coil designs, at least, the impulse test is more onerous.

articleTitle: Author's reply to discussion
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: First of all Mr Brinkworth asks why magnetic phase shift is used. I have described a well proven circuit which is in current use. Its rate of response is already higher than can be permitted from the point of view of rate of change of current which can be tolerated in machine armature circuits. We are already able to provide transistor control amplifiers for all sizes of phase shifters. The next stage is a semi-conductor type of phase shift circuit. This is developed and will be going into service in the near future. The advantage then will not be so much the fact that still faster phase shift is obtainable but that appreciably more sophisticated methods can be adopted. With very fast phase shift it is possible to dispense altogether with circulating current control on cross-connected rectifiers because immediate transference of current from, say, a rectifying to an inverting anode will be feasible.

articleTitle: Some problems of high voltage direct current power transmission
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The majority of recently published articles dealing with High Voltage D.C. Transmission have been either of general interest, involving the advantages and disadvantages of the system and descriptions of installations, or they have been for the specialist and have dealt with one specific aspect. This paper attempts to review some of the problems and possible solutions which arise once U.C. transmission has been selected for a particular installation. After an introduction giving a brief historical account of the development of this form of transmission, the major problem of inversion is considered and it is suggested that, from the point of view of flow of power, the operation of an inverter is closer to that of a rotating A.C. machine than is generally appreciated. It is shown that some source of reactive power is always required for inversion and the possible sources of this power are discussed. This reactive power influences the method of overall control of the system and also the control of the inverter grids. High-voltage mercury-arc converter valves are described as well as the influence on their performance of the circuit connections. Harmonic voltages and currents and the methods of limiting their interference with neighbouring electrical equipment are considered. In view of the fact that no H.V. D.C. circuit breakers are available, the method of protection using arc-suppression by applying a negative signal to the grids and the use of by-pass valves has been detailed. Finally a brief review is made of future developments.

articleTitle: Maynard hewitson Obituary
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Jack Hewitson, as he was always called, joined the General Post Office in 1912 as an indoor messenger, becoming an Engineer's learner in 1914 and serving an apprenticeship until 1919. He matriculated in 1921 and progressed through the engineering ranks of the Post Office to the position of Assistant Engineer in 1927, the result of success in the competitive examination for that appointment. In 1943 he was appointed Divisional Engineer, Natal, and in 1945 he returned to Head Office in charge of transmission and lines, becoming Deputy Chief Engineer in 1955, the position he held in the Post Office until he retired from the service on 13th October, 1959.
